units.translation: 11 διὰ τὸ ἀπο〈κεκορυφῶσθαι〉 or διὰ τὸ [ἀπὸ] 〈κεκορυφῶσθαι〉 from a similar passage in K : διὰ τὸ ἀπο in L : omitted in P; the ἢ, which is absent in P, should be deleted. 〈ἀπὸ τοῦ κυρωθῆναι〉 should be supplied. οἷον κύρφεις in L : οἱονεὶ κορύφεις, by syncope and metathesis and change of φ to β κύρβεις in P : οἱονεὶ κορύφεις ἢ κύρφεις κατὰ συγκοπὴν κτλ. supplied by Jacoby, Heyne 1803, 398
13 οὕτω λεγομένας added after ἀναγραφάς in L, cf. W 54

c. κύρβιας: They call κύρβεις, as Eratosthenes (fg 80 Strecker = 241 fg 37 a J.) says, the so-called ἄξονες at Athens, in which the laws are contained. But the more precise authorities say that ἄξονες are quadrangular stones, while κύρβεις are triangular; on both, laws were written at Athens. Here, however, he says κύρβιας, meaning certain tablets containing a description of the earth.
16 οἱ — περιέχοντας in P : omitted in L
d. 〈ὑγρῆς τε τραφερῆς τε:〉 of the sea and of the land. Lg
282-91 a. κέρας ὠκεανοῖο: They call 'horns of Ocean' all the rivers that flow down from it. The Ister is a river of Scythia. The sense: from afar they discerned the river and recognized it.

2 Et. Gen. (AB) κέρας: . . . κέρας is also called a river, as in Apollonius the Argonaut, e.g. IV 282-284. ἀπόρροια (καὶ ὁ ποτ. — ἀπ. in A, omitted in B). They also call κέρας all the rivers that flow down from Ocean. 19 Diod. IV 56, 3 (Timaeus)
2 κέρατα τοῦ Ὠκ. in F : Ὠκ. κέρατα in P : κέρατα with the words τοῦ Ὠκ. displaced after καταφερομένους in L

b. Ἴστρον μιν καλέ〈οντες〉: He says that the Ister flows down from the Hyperboreans and the Rhipaean mountains; and when it comes between the Scythians and Thracians it divides, and one stream flows into our sea, while the other falls into the Pontic sea [and the other into the Adriatic gulf]. He said this following Aeschylus, who says this in the Prometheus Unbound (fg 197 N.²). The Rhipaean mountains are toward the east, as Callimachus (fg 215 Schn.) says: 'from the Rhipaean mountain they send, where especially...' Eratosthenes in the third book of his Geography (fg III B 99 Berger) says that it flows from desert places and encircles the island of Peuce. Scymnus in the sixteenth book of his On Europe says only this, that the Ister is borne from desert places.

No one records that the Argonauts sailed through this river into our sea except Timagetus (fg 1 M. IV 519), whom Apollonius followed. For Scymnus says that they sailed through the Tanais to the great sea, and from there came to our sea. And he adds the digression that the Argonauts, having come to the mainland, carried the Argo on rollers until they reached the sea.
